hints: Write the full electron configuration of Cu starting from Ar, remembering it is an exception that promotes one 4s electron to give a full 3d subshell.
walkthrough:
Recall the special configuration of copper**
Copper does not follow the simple filling order. To gain the stability of a full d subshell it is $[\text{Ar}] 3\text{d}^{10} 4\text{s}^{1}$ rather than $3\text{d}^{9} 4\text{s}^{2}$. In $3\text{d}^{10}$ all five d orbitals are fully paired, so there are 0 unpaired 3d electrons, while the single $4\text{s}^{1}$ electron is unpaired.

Remove electrons to make $\text{Cu}^{2+}$**
When transition metals form ions, the 4s electrons are always lost first, then 3d. So $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ loses the $4\text{s}^{1}$ electron and one $3\text{d}$ electron to become $[\text{Ar}] 3\text{d}^{9}$. Now 4s is empty with 0 unpaired, and $3\text{d}^{9}$ has four pairs plus one single electron, so 1 unpaired.
Final answer: Cu: 3d 0 unpaired, 4s 1 unpaired; $\text{Cu}^{2+}$: 3d 1 unpaired, 4s 0 unpaired.

hints: Think what degenerate means for the five 3d orbitals when no ligands are present, and how they should appear on an energy diagram.
Recall how tetrahedral ligands split the d set into two levels, which set is higher, and whether repulsion raises or lowers the whole set compared to the isolated ion.
walkthrough:
Picture the isolated ion**
Degenerate simply means all the same energy. With no ligands around, all five 3d orbitals experience the same environment, so draw five short lines or boxes side by side on exactly the same level under isolated $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ion.

Split the orbitals in a tetrahedral field**
When four ligands approach tetrahedrally, their lone pairs repel d electrons unequally. Three d orbitals point closer to the ligands and are raised more, two point further away and are raised less. So draw a lower set of two lines and an upper set of three lines for $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ in a tetrahedral complex.

Lift the whole pattern up**
Any approach of negative ligands repels d electrons, so even the lower set is destabilised relative to the free ion. The entire split pattern must sit higher on the energy axis than the single degenerate level of the isolated ion.

Final answer: Isolated $\text{Cu}^{2+}$: five 3d orbitals at same energy (degenerate). Tetrahedral $\text{Cu}^{2+}$: split into two sets, three higher and two lower, with all five higher in energy than the isolated ion orbitals.

hints: Consider what is special about the energies of 4s and 3d electrons in transition metals that allows loss or gain of different numbers of electrons.
Think how an empty d orbital can interact with a reactant lone pair or allow temporary bonding during a catalytic cycle.
walkthrough:
Link catalysis to changing oxidation state**
A catalyst often works by lending and regaining electrons. In transition metals the 4s and 3d levels are very close in energy, so different numbers of electrons can be lost with only a small energy cost. That gives stable $+2, +3$ and other states, letting the metal cycle between them in redox catalysis.

Link catalysis to empty d orbitals**
Transition metal ions also have low lying empty d orbitals that can accept a lone pair from a reactant. This lets reactants form dative bonds to the surface or to the complex, holding them in place and weakening their internal bonds, so an intermediate with lower activation energy can form.

Final answer: Transition elements show variable / more than one stable oxidation state.
Vacant d orbitals are energetically accessible and can accept lone pairs to form dative bonds with reactants / ligands, allowing adsorption and low energy routes.

hints: Use coordination number equals number of monodentate ligands, so for $\text{Ag}^{+}$ the formula must contain two $\text{CN}^{-}$ groups.
For iron, work backwards from the overall $4-$ charge using metal oxidation state $+2$ plus $n \times (-1)$ for $n$ cyanide ligands.
walkthrough:
Complete the silver complex**
$\text{CN}^{-}$ is monodentate, so coordination number 2 means 2 ligands. The formula is $\text{Ag(CN)}_{2}$. Add charges: $(+1) + 2 \times (-1) = -1$. So the complex ion is $[\text{Ag(CN)}_{2}]^{-}$ with charge $1-$.

Deduce the iron complex**
Let the number of $\text{CN}^{-}$ be $n$. Overall charge $= (+2) + n(-1) = -4$. Solving gives $n = 6$. So coordination number $= 6$ and formula is $[\text{Fe(CN)}_{6}]^{4-}$.
Final answer: $\text{Ag}^{+}$: formula $[\text{Ag(CN)}_{2}]^{-}$, charge $1-$; $\text{Fe}^{2+}$: coordination number 6, formula $[\text{Fe(CN)}_{6}]^{4-}$.

hints: Recall the typical shape and coordination number for a 4-coordinate $\text{Au(III)}$ complex and what trans means for the positions of the two Br ligands.
Note that $\text{CN}^{-}$ can bond through C or N, so the trans structure has Br opposite Br and CN opposite NC around the central Au.
walkthrough:
Place the ligands for trans**
Draw Au in the centre with four bonds in a plane. For trans, identical ligands must be opposite. Put Br on the left and right, and put C-bonded $\text{CN}$ on one of the other sides and N-bonded $\text{NC}$ opposite it. This shows both geometrical trans arrangement and linkage difference.

Name shape and angle**
Four ligands at $90^{\circ}$ to neighbours in a flat plane is square planar. Because the two Br atoms are directly across the metal from each other, the Br-Au-Br angle is a straight line, $180^{\circ}$.
Final answer: Trans structure: central Au with Br opposite Br ($180^{\circ}$ apart) and CN opposite NC, all in one plane. Shape square planar, Br-Au-Br bond angle $180^{\circ}$.

hints: Start from the titration data to find moles of $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ using $n = c \times V$ with volume in $\text{dm}^{3}$.
Use the given equation $3\text{MnO}_{4}^{-} : 5\text{V}^{2+}$ to convert moles of manganate to moles of $\text{V}^{2+}$, which equals moles of V atoms in the sample.
Convert moles of V to mass using $A_{r} = 50.9$ and then express as a percentage of the $0.250 \text{ g}$ sample.
walkthrough:
Find moles of $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ used**
Use $n = cV$. Convert $22.5 \text{ cm}^{3}$ to $\text{dm}^{3}$ by dividing by 1000:
$$n(\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}) = 0.0750 \times \frac{22.5}{1000} = 1.6875 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$

Convert to moles of $\text{V}^{2+}$**
From the equation, $3$ mol $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ reacts with $5$ mol $\text{V}^{2+}$:
$$n(\text{V}^{2+}) = \frac{5}{3} \times 1.6875 \times 10^{-3} = 2.8125 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$
All this $\text{V}^{2+}$ came from the vanadium in the $0.250 \text{ g}$ sample, so moles V $= 2.8125 \times 10^{-3}$ mol.

Calculate mass and percentage**
$$m(\text{V}) = 2.8125 \times 10^{-3} \times 50.9 = 0.143 \text{ g}$$
$$\% \text{V} = \frac{0.143}{0.250} \times 100 = 57.3\%$$
Keep at least 2 significant figures to match the data.

hints: Compare oxidation numbers to find total electrons gained per $\text{VO}_{3}^{-}$ ($+5$ to $+2$) and electrons lost per Zn, then find the simplest $\text{VO}_{3}^{-}$ : Zn ratio.
Balance O with $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ and then H with $\text{H}^{+}$ under acidic conditions, checking charge balances on both sides.
walkthrough:
Get the electron ratio**
V goes from $+5$ in $\text{VO}_{3}^{-}$ to $+2$ in $\text{V}^{2+}$, a gain of 3 electrons. Zn goes from $0$ to $+2$, a loss of 2 electrons. To equalise electrons, $2 \times 3 = 3 \times 2 = 6$ electrons, so you need $2\text{VO}_{3}^{-}$ for every $3\text{Zn}$.

Finish balancing with acid**
With $2\text{VO}_{3}^{-}$ you have 6 O atoms, so add $6\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ on the right. That gives 12 H on the right, so add $12\text{H}^{+}$ on the left. Check charge: left $(-2 +12) = +10$, right $(+4 +6) = +10$. The balanced equation is:
$$2\text{VO}_{3}^{-} + 3\text{Zn} + 12\text{H}^{+} \rightarrow 2\text{V}^{2+} + 3\text{Zn}^{2+} + 6\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$
